transcript:
HEADER
Date: 2026-04-09
Start: 16:17 UTC
Duration: 52m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Aisha Grant (Clearline Head of ML), Ben Morales (Clearline SRE), Priya Nair (Product), Tom Reeves (CTO)
Meeting ID: ff-20260409-rcp-0317

AUTO SUMMARY (auto-generated, may be fuzzy): Agreed to pilot charter focusing on TTFT p95 <= 250ms and TPOT p95 <= 12ms/token for short responses; measurement plan to include warm/cold runs and 3 traffic profiles. Action items captured.

TRANSCRIPT BODY:
[00:00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. This is Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on this account, with Ravi and Jordan. How's everyone doing?
[00:00:08] Aisha Grant: Doing well, thanks. We wanted to use today to lock down acceptance criteria for the pilot -- particularly latency vs throughput trade offs.
[00:00:16] Ravi Patel: Great, yeah. We sent over a short note about TTFT and TPOT definitions earlier, but maybe we can align on exact measurement definitions so the benchmark is apples-to-apples.
[00:00:26] Ben Morales: Quick one up front — we run a mix of synchronous chat and async summarization. So latency matters for chat, throughput matters for nightly batch summarization.
[00:00:35] Jordan Lee: Totally. For the call, TTFT = time to first token, from request arrival to first byte. TPOT we define as time per output token, basically per-token emit latency — makes sense? (laughs) We sometimes see it called TPT or TPOT in docs.
[00:00:50] Tom Reeves: Yep, that naming's fine. I just want clear pass/fail gates.
[00:00:55] Maya Chen: Proposed pilot acceptance criteria — for chat endpoints: TTFT p95 <= 250ms, p99 <= 500ms. For steady-state token emission: TPOT p95 <= 12ms/token, p99 <= 25ms/token for medium-length outputs. For batch/throughput use case, we target sustained TPOT throughput of 60k tokens/min under dedicated capacity.
[00:01:17] Priya Nair: Those numbers seem aggressive. Can you show a baseline comparison to our current provider? Right now, our observed TTFT p95 is about 420ms.
[00:01:27] Maya Chen: Sure — that's why the pilot. We expect improvements with prefix caching and batching policies. We'll provide side-by-side runs.
[00:01:34] Aisha Grant: Important: our prompts vary a lot. We have three buckets: short (<=64 tokens), medium (65-512), long (>512). Traffic mix roughly 35% short, 50% medium, 15% long. Ben, does that match infra's numbers?
[00:01:48] Ben Morales: Yes, that's accurate; peak rps during day is ~280 req/s but token throughput spikes during scheduled jobs.
[00:01:56] Ravi Patel: Good to know. For the benchmark we'll need the histogram and a few representative prompts per bucket. Also, we need to decide cache warm-up policy: do we measure cold-start TTFT separately? We recommend three phases: cold (no cache, scale-from-zero), warm (prefix cache populated), and steady-state with batching.
[00:02:14] Aisha Grant: We want both measured. Cold-start matters for traffic spikes. But pass/fail should be on warm and steady-state, cold will be informative.
[00:02:23] Jordan Lee: Agreed. Also note that TPOT is sensitive to quantization/model variant; if you run an int8 variant we can get better TPOT but results may vary on output quality. We should flag quality regression tests as part of acceptance.
[00:02:37] Tom Reeves: Yes — quality gate is mandatory. We can use the existing prompt-anchored eval set.
[00:02:42] Maya Chen: Actionable measurement plan I propose: 1) Redwood will run a baseline run on hosted infra with customer's prompt set and traffic mix; 2) run three phases (cold/warm/steady) and capture p50/p95/p99 TTFT and p50/p95/p99 TPOT, plus tokens/s, error rates, and cost per 1M tokens; 3) capture trace-level logs for 1 hour at peak to verify KV cache hits and batching stats.
[00:03:05] Ben Morales: What tool are you planning to use for load? We prefer something we can run in our infra for the final run.
[00:03:11] Ravi Patel: We'll provide a Locust harness and a lightweight Go loadgen. You can run either locally. For transparency we'll run a mirrored harness from our side and share raw logs. Note: some transcription notes from earlier runs — sometimes fireflies scribbles 'K-V cash' (laughs) — we're not perfect.
[00:03:26] Aisha Grant: (laughs) fine. On SLOs: what about p99 for TTFT? You proposed 500ms earlier. How strict is that?
[00:03:33] Maya Chen: p99 500ms is a negotiated stretch target. Pass/fail we'll use p95 primarily but we'll report p99 as severity metric. If p99 is high but p95 meets target we still consider pilot successful but recommend mitigation for tail via autoscaling and routing policies.
[00:03:48] Priya Nair: For batch summarization, do we measure TPOT differently? It's not latency sensitive per request but total throughput per minute matters.
[00:03:55] Jordan Lee: Right — for batch use case we define throughput acceptance as sustained token throughput with TPOT averaged over 5m windows. For example, target 60k tokens/min at p95, with error rate <0.5%. We'll also capture GPU occupancy and memory metrics.
[00:04:11] Ben Morales: Regarding private deployment: we might try both hosted and dedicated. Dedicated will give more predictable TPOT. Is that part of the pilot?
[00:04:19] Maya Chen: We scoped two tracks: hosted quick-run to validate TTFT improvements (7-day window), and optional dedicated trial if you want to lock throughput (14-day). We'll confirm which track after the first baseline run.
[00:04:30] Tom Reeves: Ok. Timeline wise we're trying to commit to Q2 infra changes; can you run the first benchmark within 7 days?
[00:04:36] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll aim for a Redwood-hosted run in 5 business days pending prompt set and histogram.
[00:04:41] Aisha Grant: One more: telemetry and auditing. We need request-level audit logs, SSO and KMS integration for the dedicated run. Can you provide SOC2 attestation and KMS wiring docs?
[00:04:52] Ravi Patel: Absolutely. We'll attach SOC2 and our KMS integration guide. For the dedicated/private flows we'll include network diagrams and example SAML configs.
[00:04:59] Priya Nair: Any competitors' benchmarks we should be aware of? We saw vendor claims from OpenAI showing low TTFT on small prompts, but they lacked detailed token distribution.
[00:05:08] Jordan Lee: We'll include a comparison table with our runs vs public numbers where applicable. Remember public numbers can be synthetic.
[00:05:14] Ben Morales: For the measurement dashboard, can we have live traces and aggregated histograms?
[00:05:19] Ravi Patel: Yes — we'll ship a Grafana dashboard that shows p50/p95/p99 TTFT, TPOT histograms, batch size distribution, KV cache hit rate, GPU occupancy and error rates.
[00:05:28] Maya Chen: Recap of acceptance and pass/fail: Primary gating metric = TTFT p95 <= 250ms on warm traffic mix for chat endpoints. Secondary gating metric = TPOT p95 <= 12ms/token for medium outputs or sustained throughput target for batch jobs. Must pass quality guardrails (no >4% delta in core accuracy eval).
[00:05:46] Tom Reeves: That sounds reasonable. We'll try to provision sample data by Wednesday.
[00:05:50] Aisha Grant: Two quick clarifications — how do you measure tokenization differences between our tokenizer and yours? Token counts can vary and affect TPOT.
[00:05:58] Jordan Lee: Good call. We'll normalize by running both tokenizers on the prompt set and report token delta. For reporting we'll publish both raw tokens and normalized tokens per run.
[00:06:07] Priya Nair: Final ask: include cost estimate per 1M tokens for each model variant used so we can weigh latency vs cost.
[00:06:13] Maya Chen: We'll include a cost breakdown in the worksheet.
[00:06:18] Ben Morales: Ok, good meeting.
[00:06:20] Maya Chen: Great, thanks everyone. We'll send the pilot charter and benchmark instructions after this call.
[00:06:25] Aisha Grant: Thanks, talk soon.

(Transcript continues with short Q&A and time stamps showing some cross talk; auto captions show occasional mis-hearings such as 'K-V cash' vs 'KV cache', 'TPOT' as 'T-POT', and speaker attribution flips).

END OF TRANSCRIPT
